questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids in an elderly smoker suggests:
questions.concept: Mechanical obstruction causes dysphagia first to solids progressing to liquids with weight loss, whereas motility disorders such as achalasia cause dysphagia to both from the outset. Endoscopy with biopsy is the investigation of choice.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Achalasia cardia is characterised manometrically by:
options: Failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter with absent peristalsis
questions.concept: Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons produces a non-relaxing hypertensive sphincter with aperistalsis, giving a bird-beak appearance on barium swallow. Pneumatic dilatation, Heller myotomy or POEM are treatment options.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Barrett oesophagus is:
options: Intestinal (columnar) metaplasia of the lower oesophagus predisposing to adenocarcinoma
questions.concept: Chronic acid reflux replaces squamous with specialised intestinal columnar epithelium, a premalignant change for adenocarcinoma requiring endoscopic surveillance; dysplasia is treated by radiofrequency ablation or resection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome comprises:
options: Dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia and a postcricoid oesophageal web
questions.concept: This syndrome of middle-aged women is a recognised premalignant condition for postcricoid squamous carcinoma. Iron replacement and dilatation of the web relieve symptoms.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: The commonest histological type of gastric carcinoma is:
questions.concept: Over 90% of gastric malignancies are adenocarcinoma, classified by Lauren into intestinal type, related to Helicobacter pylori and atrophic gastritis, and diffuse type with signet ring cells producing linitis plastica.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Virchow node, an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node in gastric carcinoma, indicates:
options: Advanced disease with distant nodal metastasis
questions.concept: Troisier sign, a palpable Virchow node, indicates metastatic spread via the thoracic duct and inoperability. Other signs of advanced disease are Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg tumours and Blumer shelf.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Helicobacter pylori eradication is important in gastric disease because it:
options: Reduces peptic ulcer recurrence and the risk of gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma
questions.concept: H. pylori is a class I carcinogen causing chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma; eradication with triple or quadruple therapy heals ulcers, prevents recurrence and can regress early MALT lymphoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Krukenberg tumour refers to:
options: Bilateral ovarian metastases with signet ring cells, classically from gastric carcinoma
questions.concept: Transcoelomic and lymphatic spread from a gastric or colonic signet ring adenocarcinoma produces bilateral solid ovarian metastases with mucin-filled signet ring cells in a cellular stroma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: Boerhaave syndrome is:
options: Spontaneous full-thickness oesophageal rupture after forceful vomiting
A mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction
questions.concept: Full-thickness rupture, usually of the left posterolateral distal oesophagus, causes severe chest pain, surgical emphysema and mediastinitis with high mortality. Mallory-Weiss tears are mucosal only and usually stop bleeding spontaneously.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Oesophagus, stomach & gastric carcinoma
questions.stem: A pharyngeal (Zenker) pouch arises through:
options: Killian dehiscence between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
questions.concept: A pulsion diverticulum herniates posteriorly through Killian dehiscence due to cricopharyngeal incoordination, causing dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis and gurgling. Endoscopic stapling or diverticulectomy with myotomy is curative.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: The commonest site of colorectal carcinoma is:
questions.concept: About two-thirds of colorectal cancers arise in the rectosigmoid. Left-sided tumours present with obstruction and altered bowel habit with bleeding, while right-sided lesions present with anaemia and a mass because the lumen is wider and stool liquid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Familial adenomatous polyposis is characterised by:
options: Autosomal dominant APC mutation with hundreds of colonic adenomas and near-certain malignancy
questions.concept: APC mutation on chromosome 5q causes hundreds to thousands of adenomas from adolescence with virtually 100% cancer risk by age 40, so prophylactic colectomy is required. Gardner and Turcot syndromes are variants.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Hirschsprung disease is confirmed by:
options: Rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks
questions.concept: Full-thickness or suction rectal biopsy demonstrating aganglionosis in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses with hypertrophied cholinergic nerve trunks is diagnostic. Barium enema shows a transition zone and a reversed rectosigmoid index.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: The classical presentation of a fissure-in-ano is:
options: Severe pain during and after defecation with bright red bleeding streaking the stool
questions.concept: An anal fissure, most often in the posterior midline, causes intense pain from sphincter spasm with minimal bright bleeding. Chronic fissures show a sentinel tag and hypertrophied papilla; treatment is stool softeners and topical diltiazem or GTN.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Goodsall rule relates to:
options: Predicting the course of an anal fistula tract from its external opening
questions.concept: Goodsall rule states that an external opening anterior to the transverse anal line tracks radially to the anal canal, while a posterior opening curves to open in the posterior midline. Horseshoe fistulas follow the posterior pattern.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Second-degree haemorrhoids are defined as those that:
options: Prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously
questions.concept: First degree bleed without prolapse, second prolapse and reduce spontaneously, third need manual reduction and fourth are irreducible. Treatment escalates from diet and banding to haemorrhoidectomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening complication of:
options: Ulcerative colitis and Clostridioides difficile colitis
questions.concept: Transverse colon dilatation beyond 6 cm with systemic toxicity complicates severe colitis; barium enema and colonoscopy are contraindicated because of perforation risk. Failure to improve within 48 to 72 hours mandates colectomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis?
options: Transmural skip lesions with non-caseating granulomas and fistulae
Continuous mucosal disease from the rectum
questions.concept: Crohn disease is transmural with skip lesions anywhere from mouth to anus, granulomas, cobblestoning, strictures and fistulae, while ulcerative colitis is continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum proximally with crypt abscesses and pseudopolyps.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Sigmoid volvulus characteristically shows which radiological sign?
options: Coffee-bean or omega loop sign on plain abdominal radiograph
questions.concept: A massively distended sigmoid loop arising from the pelvis produces the coffee-bean appearance. Initial management is endoscopic decompression with a flatus tube, and elective sigmoid resection prevents recurrence unless gangrene demands urgent surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Colon, rectum & anal canal disorders
questions.stem: Carcinoembryonic antigen in colorectal carcinoma is most useful for:
questions.concept: CEA lacks sensitivity and specificity for screening or diagnosis, but a rising level after curative resection is a sensitive marker of recurrence. Screening is by faecal occult blood testing and colonoscopy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Painless gross haematuria in an adult smoker should be investigated primarily for:
options: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the bladder
questions.concept: Painless visible haematuria is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, especially in smokers and those exposed to aniline dyes and aromatic amines. Cystoscopy with upper tract imaging is mandatory.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: The classical triad of renal cell carcinoma is:
options: Haematuria, flank pain and a palpable mass, present in only a minority
questions.concept: The complete triad occurs in under 10% and indicates advanced disease. Renal cell carcinoma is notable for paraneoplastic syndromes - polycythaemia, hypercalcaemia, Stauffer syndrome - and spread along the renal vein into the inferior vena cava.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: The commonest testicular tumour in a young adult male is:
questions.concept: Seminoma peaks at 30 to 40 years, is radiosensitive with excellent prognosis and may raise placental alkaline phosphatase but not alpha-fetoprotein. A raised AFP indicates a non-seminomatous element regardless of histology reported.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: The correct approach for a suspected testicular tumour is:
options: Inguinal orchidectomy with high cord ligation, never trans-scrotal biopsy
questions.concept: A trans-scrotal approach violates lymphatic drainage planes and risks scrotal skin and inguinal node contamination, altering the pattern of spread. Tumour markers AFP, beta-hCG and LDH are taken before orchidectomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: A hydrocele is best distinguished from an inguinoscrotal hernia by:
options: Ability to get above the swelling with a positive transillumination test
questions.concept: In a hydrocele the examining fingers can get above the swelling and it transilluminates brilliantly, whereas an inguinoscrotal hernia extends up into the inguinal canal with a cough impulse and may be reducible with bowel sounds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Sudden severe testicular pain in an adolescent with a high-riding transverse testis and absent cremasteric reflex indicates:
options: Testicular torsion requiring emergency exploration within six hours
questions.concept: Torsion is a surgical emergency as salvage falls sharply after 6 hours. A negative Prehn sign and absent cremasteric reflex favour torsion over epididymo-orchitis; exploration should not be delayed for imaging when suspicion is high.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: A left-sided varicocele of sudden onset in an older man should raise suspicion of:
options: Left renal carcinoma obstructing the left testicular vein
questions.concept: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, so a renal tumour invading it can obstruct drainage causing a new varicocele that does not empty on lying down. Ultrasound of the kidneys is indicated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Phimosis in an adult may predispose to:
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the penis
questions.concept: Chronic inflammation with retained smegma and inability to retract the foreskin is a risk factor for penile squamous carcinoma; neonatal circumcision is strongly protective. HPV infection is another important risk factor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Paraphimosis is a urological emergency because:
options: The retracted tight foreskin forms a constricting band causing glans oedema and ischaemia
questions.concept: A retracted phimotic ring acts as a tourniquet, producing progressive oedema and eventual necrosis of the glans. Manual reduction after compression, or a dorsal slit if that fails, is required urgently.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: The commonest composition of urinary calculi is:
questions.concept: Calcium oxalate accounts for about 70 to 80% of stones and is radio-opaque. Struvite (triple phosphate) stones form staghorn calculi with urease-producing Proteus infection, while uric acid stones are radiolucent and dissolve with urinary alkalinisation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Intermittent claudication is characterised by:
options: Calf pain on walking a fixed distance, relieved by rest
Pain at rest relieved by walking
Pain only at night in bed
questions.concept: Claudication is reproducible exercise-induced muscle ischaemia relieved within minutes of rest. Progression to rest pain, typically in the forefoot at night and relieved by hanging the leg down, indicates critical limb ischaemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: An ankle-brachial pressure index below 0.4 indicates:
questions.concept: An ABPI of 0.9 to 1.2 is normal, 0.5 to 0.9 indicates claudication and below 0.4 critical ischaemia. Falsely high values above 1.3 occur with calcified incompressible vessels in diabetes and chronic kidney disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: The six Ps of acute limb ischaemia include all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: The six Ps are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and perishing cold. Paralysis and sensory loss indicate a threatened limb requiring urgent revascularisation within about six hours.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) characteristically affects:
options: Young male smokers, involving small and medium arteries of the limbs
questions.concept: Thromboangiitis obliterans is a segmental inflammatory thrombotic occlusion of small and medium vessels in young male heavy smokers, with migratory thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon. Absolute smoking cessation is the only effective treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: A venous ulcer characteristically occurs:
options: In the gaiter area above the medial malleolus with surrounding lipodermatosclerosis
On the tips of the toes
Over the lateral malleolus with a punched-out edge
On the heel with painless deep necrosis
questions.concept: Venous hypertension produces a shallow sloping ulcer in the gaiter area with haemosiderin pigmentation, varicose eczema and lipodermatosclerosis. Graduated compression after excluding arterial disease by ABPI is the mainstay.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: The Trendelenburg test in varicose veins assesses:
options: Incompetence of the saphenofemoral junction and perforator valves
questions.concept: After emptying the leg and occluding the saphenofemoral junction, rapid filling from above on release indicates junctional incompetence, while filling from below with the tourniquet in place indicates incompetent perforators. Perthes test assesses deep venous patency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is generally considered for elective repair when its diameter exceeds:
questions.concept: Rupture risk rises steeply above 5.5 cm, at which point elective open or endovascular repair outweighs operative risk. Smaller aneurysms are monitored by ultrasound surveillance with blood pressure and smoking control.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: The classical triad of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is:
options: Abdominal or back pain, hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass
questions.concept: This triad in an older man demands immediate transfer to theatre; misdiagnosis as renal colic is a classic pitfall. Permissive hypotension is maintained until proximal control is achieved.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Subclavian steal syndrome results from:
options: Proximal subclavian stenosis causing retrograde vertebral artery flow with arm exercise
questions.concept: Stenosis proximal to the vertebral origin causes blood to be siphoned retrogradely down the vertebral artery to supply the arm during exercise, producing posterior circulation symptoms - dizziness, diplopia, syncope - with a blood pressure difference between arms.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: The most important investigation before surgery for varicose veins is:
options: Duplex ultrasound to map incompetence and confirm deep venous patency
questions.concept: Duplex ultrasound identifies the sites of reflux and confirms the deep system is patent, since stripping superficial veins in a patient with deep venous obstruction would be harmful.
